description: PHASEWAKE is a multidisciplinary Technion team with backgrounds in computer science, physics, aerospace engineering, and GIS. For “Dancing with the SARs,” we aim to use NISAR radar data to detect and clearly visualize changes on Earth’s surface. Our team is complete; this listing is open only so our existing teammates can join officially.
summary:
PhaseWake helps emergency coordinators and affected communities understand road access after floods. When roads are damaged and ground reports are scarce, dated satellite evidence can help identify where inspections are needed.

For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we built a mobile-first web application using NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV radar data distributed by ASF DAAC. Our Python pipeline compares compatible before/after observations within each radar track, detects changes in radar brightness and combines road assessments across tracks. We link this evidence to OpenStreetMap roads.

Users can search for destinations, compare routes that penalise potentially affected and unknown roads, explore mapped facilities and inspect before/after imagery. Evidence cards show observation dates, overlap and coverage, keeping uncertainty visible.

Our Nepal Trishuli River demonstration flags 170 road segments covering 30.65 km as potentially affected. These are provisional screening results, not confirmed damage or verified passable routes. Separately sourced, dated field reports can add context between satellite observations.

By connecting satellite analysis to specific roads and route comparisons, PhaseWake aims to help responders prioritise inspections and make better-informed access decisions.
details:
PhaseWake helps emergency coordinators and road engineers assess road access after floods and prioritise field inspections. It connects satellite observations to individual road segments and route comparisons, making the supporting evidence, observation dates and uncertainty visible.

We use NASA–ISRO NISAR Level 2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) radar data distributed through ASF DAAC. Our Python pipeline compares compatible before-and-after observations within each radar track, checks alignment and usable coverage, calculates HH/HV radar-brightness change and identifies potential overlap with OpenStreetMap roads. It then combines road assessments from the tracks that observed each segment. Our Nepal demonstration uses three radar tracks, with the primary comparison covering 19 and 31 August 2026.

The current analysis flags 170 mapped road segments covering 30.65 kilometres as potentially affected. These are provisional screening results, not independently confirmed damaged or closed roads. Evidence cards show acquisition dates, overlap, coverage and interpretation limits so users can understand why a segment needs closer investigation.

We built a mobile-first web application using React, TypeScript, TanStack Start and Leaflet. Users can choose a start point, search for destinations, explore mapped facilities, compare before-and-after imagery and review up to three route options. Browser-based routing penalises potentially affected and unknown road evidence while displaying distance and route warnings.

A separate community-reporting layer allows dated observations about flooding, debris, closures, restored access and facility availability. Reports remain anonymous and unverified. Expiry, voting, device-count rules and rate limiting help manage submissions but do not establish their truth or authenticate reporters. Community observations supplement satellite evidence between acquisitions without replacing the original radar assessment.

Our creative contribution is the combination of multiple NISAR views, transparent road evidence and route comparisons within one accessible workflow. We considered satellite timing gaps, different acquisition geometries, incomplete road mapping, uncertain causes of radar change and the need for a simple interface during stressful situations.

Radar change does not establish physical damage or current passability. Routes do not model vehicle suitability, one-way restrictions, travel times or authoritative live closures. Unmapped connections and mapped facilities require independent checking. The application does not certify safe evacuation routes or dispatch emergency services.

Our intended impact is to help response teams identify where further inspection is most useful. The next proposed step is a pilot with a road or disaster-management authority, measuring inspection-planning time and independently verified outcomes against its existing workflow, followed by validation on additional disaster events.
